title: Attend to dairy parlour water treatment and waste water

lessons.title: Clean water for the parlour
lessons.html:
Why water quality matters in a dairy

Water touches everything in the parlour: the milking plant, the bulk tank, the teats and the cows' drinking troughs. Dirty or hard water can put bacteria into the milk, make detergents work poorly and leave milkstone in the pipes. Milk buyers expect the farm to use clean water of drinking quality for cleaning milk equipment.

Common water problems on SA farms

ProblemEffect
Bacteria (from dams, rivers or dirty tanks)High bacteria counts in milk
Hard water (lots of calcium and magnesium, common in borehole water)Scale and milkstone, detergents work less well
Iron and manganeseBrown stains and deposits in pipes
Mud and siltBlocked filters, dirty equipment

Treating water

The farm may use one or more of these:

  • Filters to remove sand and silt. Clean or change them as the supplier says.
  • Chlorination by a dosing pump or tablets to kill bacteria. Check that the doser is working and the chemical drum is not empty.
  • Water softening or adjusting the detergent programme for hard water, as advised by the detergent supplier.
  • UV units that kill bacteria with light. The lamp must be on and the glass clean.

Your daily tasks

  1. Check that dosing pumps and filters are working.
  2. Check water storage tanks are covered so birds and animals cannot get in.
  3. Record checks in the water log.
  4. Take water samples when the manager asks, using clean sample bottles from the laboratory.
  5. Report any change in colour, smell or taste of the water.

Handle chlorine carefully. Wear gloves and goggles, store it away from acids and never mix it with acid cleaners.

lessons.title: Managing dairy waste water
lessons.html:
Where does the parlour water go?

Every milking produces a lot of dirty water: dung and urine washed off the floor, milk residues, and cleaning water with detergents. This waste water is rich in nutrients and bacteria. If it runs into rivers, dams or groundwater it pollutes them, kills fish and can make people and animals ill downstream.

The law

The National Water Act 36 of 1998 protects water resources. Farms must not pollute rivers, streams or groundwater, and using or disposing of waste water may need to be authorised. The farm manager is responsible for the permits, but every worker must help keep waste water inside the system.

A typical waste water system

  1. Scraping solid dung off yards before hosing, to use less water.
  2. Solids trap or separator to catch sand and solids.
  3. Ponds or lagoons where water settles and breaks down.
  4. Irrigation of the diluted water onto pasture or crop lands, as planned by the manager, so nutrients are used as fertiliser.

Daily good practice

  • Scrape before you hose. Use only the water you need.
  • Keep sand traps and channels clear so they do not overflow.
  • Check pond levels. Report if ponds are nearly full, especially before rain.
  • Never let waste water run into a stream, vlei or dam.
  • Never pump spilt milk, chemicals or dead animals into the waste ponds without permission.
  • Only irrigate effluent where and when the manager says. Do not irrigate onto waterlogged soil or just before heavy rain.

Safety around ponds

Effluent ponds are deep and slippery. Do not swim, and work in pairs near ponds. Keep children and animals out. Wash hands after handling effluent and before eating.

Key points

  • Use clean water of drinking quality for cleaning milk equipment.
  • Check filters, dosing pumps and water tanks daily and record the checks.
  • Scrape before hosing to save water.
  • Keep waste water out of rivers, dams and groundwater as the National Water Act requires.
  • Report full ponds or overflowing channels straight away.
